Read the sheets or tables of an Excel workbook

Source: R/read_workbook.R
read_workbook.Rd

Reads every sheet of a workbook into a named list, finding the table on each sheet, or the sheets, ranges or defined Excel tables you choose. Warns when cells outside what was read are left behind.

Usage

read_workbook(
  path,
  sheet = NULL,
  range = NULL,
  table = NULL,
  check = TRUE,
  ...
)

Arguments

path

Path to an Excel file (.xlsx, .xlsm or .xls).

sheet

Sheet names or positions. NULL (default) reads every sheet.

range

The area to read, where the default NULL finds the table on each sheet. One range, such as "B3:F40" (with a single sheet) or "Sheet1!B3:F40"; or one per sheet as a named vector, c(Sheet1 = "B3:F40", Sheet2 = NA), where NA means find the table. Sheets not named are found automatically.

A range can also be a named range from the workbook (Formulas > Name Manager), such as "Sales". A name carries its own sheet, so range = c("Sales", "Costs") reads both, named by the names, wherever they are; in a per-sheet vector the name must lie on that sheet. Named ranges need an .xlsx file and the xml2 package.

table

Names of defined Excel tables, or TRUE for all of them. Cannot be combined with sheet or range. .xlsx and .xlsm only.

check

If TRUE (default), warn about cells outside what was read.

...

Passed on to readxl::read_excel(), such as col_types, na or skip. skip is applied before the table is found.

Value

A tibble when a single sheet, range or table is named; otherwise a named list of tibbles, also when the workbook has only one sheet, so the shape depends on the call and not on the file.

Details

Sheets. With sheet = NULL (default), every sheet is read and the result is a list named by sheet. Name or number the sheets to read only those.

Finding the table. Without a range, readxl reads the smallest rectangle around all non-empty cells, so a title becomes the header, a note below the table becomes extra rows, and a comment to the right becomes a column named ...7. read_workbook() instead finds the table on each sheet, the largest block of cells not split by an entirely empty row or column, with title rows on top left out (see inspect_excel()), and reads only that. Whatever lies outside is not read, and a warning lists it, except titles above the table, which are expected.

Speed. Everything is read by readxl's C++ reader: each sheet once as text to find the table, and once more for the table itself with proper column types. That is about twice a plain readxl::read_excel(), for .xlsx and .xls alike. Give range and check = FALSE to read with a single call.

Passwords. A workbook with a password to open is encrypted, and readxl cannot read it; read_workbook() says so instead of failing with a zip error. Sheet or workbook protection without a password to open does not encrypt the file and reads as usual.

Choosing the area yourself. range takes one range for one sheet, or a named vector with one range per sheet, where NA (or leaving a sheet out) means find the table. table reads defined Excel tables (Insert > Table) by name, or all of them with table = TRUE. A table keeps its range when rows are added in Excel, which a hard-coded range does not, so prefer it when the workbook has one. A table's totals row is not read. readxl has no support for tables; their ranges are looked up in the file and read as ranges.

See also

inspect_excel() for the check on its own, read_files() to read many files at once.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# Every sheet, the table found on each, as a named list:
sheets <- read_workbook("data/report.xlsx")

# One sheet, as a tibble:
df <- read_workbook("data/report.xlsx", sheet = "2024")

# Your own range, for one sheet or per sheet (NA: find it):
df     <- read_workbook("data/report.xlsx", range = "2024!B3:F40")
sheets <- read_workbook("data/report.xlsx", range = c(`2024` = "B3:F40", `2023` = NA))

# Named ranges (Formulas > Name Manager), wherever they are:
sales  <- read_workbook("data/report.xlsx", range = "Sales")
parts  <- read_workbook("data/report.xlsx", range = c("Sales", "Costs"))

# A defined table, or all of them:
sales  <- read_workbook("data/report.xlsx", table = "Sales")
tables <- read_workbook("data/report.xlsx", table = TRUE)
} # }
